## Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

### Depth: Communicating Across Levels

Designing with data aims to reduce reliance on “gut” decisions, thereby breaking hierarchical decision-making structures. In a data-literate environment, top-down, hunch-based management cannot thrive; instead, well-formulated questions invite discussion, challenge, and the possibility of being wrong. User data—gathered through A/B testing, ethnographic research, prototypes, surveys, usability studies, and more—drives decisions with less risk than executive hunches.

An early 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO,” captured this principle: data resolves conflicts without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, described how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation. Patty McCord, Netflix’s Chief Talent Officer for over 12 years, emphasized that having a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for your customers gives more people a voice in product development.

At Netflix, the data-driven approach was universally accepted—from CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt down to individual contributors. Patty McCord noted that even the CEO does not get to do whatever he wants; everyone can get caught up in thinking they know the answer. A/B testing mitigates top-down problem-solving because everyone learns from experimentation. When Reed Hastings had a strong product idea, he submitted it to the same rigorous A/B testing as everyone else. On rare occasions, he might dictate an exact approach, but only on “his test cell”—the experimental group he backed. That cell was tested against others proposed by the product team. If it didn’t win, it didn’t launch. Upper management holding themselves accountable to the same process reinforced subjecting ideas to grounded review through experimentation, and treating “failure” as a positive outcome.

Shifting to a data-aware framework requires examining how product and design decisions have been made. If decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, those people must understand and recognize the value of bringing user data into the process, because their individual weight will diminish—as will the weight of any single opinion. This also prompts self-reflection: are you comfortable seeing how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process?

## Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

### Depth: Communicating Across Levels

Designing with data aims to reduce reliance on “gut” decisions, thereby breaking hierarchical decision-making structures. In a traditional hierarchy, decisions often flow from the highest-paid person’s opinion (HiPPO). Data introduces an objective arbiter: when decisions are based on empirical evidence rather than authority, the hierarchy flattens. In a data-literate environment, top-down, hunch-based management cannot thrive; instead, well-formulated questions invite discussion, challenge, and the possibility of being wrong. User data—gathered through A/B testing, ethnographic research, prototypes, surveys, usability studies, and more—drives decisions with less risk than executive hunches. This shift from subjective intuition to objective evidence reduces the influence of any single individual’s opinion, distributing decision-making power more evenly across the organization.

An early 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO,” captured this principle: data resolves conflicts without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics. When disagreements arise, an A/B test can provide a clear, measurable outcome that settles the matter based on user behavior, not on who has more seniority. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, described how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation: because anyone could propose and test an idea, the best solutions could emerge from anywhere in the company, not just from the executive suite. Patty McCord, Netflix’s Chief Talent Officer for over 12 years, emphasized that having a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for your customers gives more people a voice in product development. This mechanism shifts the basis of argument from authority to evidence, enabling junior team members to challenge senior ones if the data supports their view.

At Netflix, the data-driven approach was universally accepted—from CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt down to individual contributors. This universal commitment meant that everyone, regardless of rank, was subject to the same evidentiary standards. Patty McCord noted that even the CEO does not get to do whatever he wants; everyone can get caught up in thinking they know the answer. A/B testing mitigates top-down problem-solving because everyone learns from experimentation. When Reed Hastings had a strong product idea, he submitted it to the same rigorous A/B testing as everyone else. On rare occasions, he might dictate an exact approach, but only on “his test cell”—the experimental group he backed. That cell was tested against others proposed by the product team. If it didn’t win, it didn’t launch. This practice treated the CEO’s idea as a hypothesis to be tested, not a directive to be followed. Upper management holding themselves accountable to the same process reinforced subjecting ideas to grounded review through experimentation, and treating “failure” as a positive outcome—a learning opportunity rather than a personal defeat.

Shifting to a data-aware framework requires examining how product and design decisions have been made. If decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, those people must understand and recognize the value of bringing user data into the process, because their individual weight will diminish—as will the weight of any single opinion. This transition demands that individuals separate their ego from their ideas and prioritize customer outcomes over personal credit. It also prompts self-reflection: are you comfortable seeing how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process? Embracing data means accepting that your intuition, however experienced, may be wrong, and that the ultimate arbiter is the user’s behavior, not your conviction.

## Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

### Depth: Communicating Across Levels

Designing with data aims to reduce reliance on “gut” decisions, thereby breaking hierarchical decision-making structures. In a traditional hierarchy, decisions often flow from the highest-paid person’s opinion (HiPPO). Data introduces an objective arbiter: when decisions are based on empirical evidence rather than authority, the hierarchy flattens. In a data-literate environment, top-down, hunch-based management cannot thrive; instead, well-formulated questions invite discussion, challenge, and the possibility of being wrong. User data—gathered through A/B testing, ethnographic research, prototypes, surveys, usability studies, and more—drives decisions with less risk than executive hunches. This shift from subjective intuition to objective evidence reduces the influence of any single individual’s opinion, distributing decision-making power more evenly across the organization.

An early 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, “Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO,” captured this principle: data resolves conflicts without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics. When disagreements arise, an A/B test can provide a clear, measurable outcome that settles the matter based on user behavior, not on who has more seniority. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, described how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation: because anyone could propose and test an idea, the best solutions could emerge from anywhere in the company, not just from the executive suite. If it didn’t win, it didn’t launch. This practice treated the CEO’s idea as a hypothesis to be tested, not a directive to be followed. Upper management holding themselves accountable to the same process reinforced subjecting ideas to grounded review through experimentation, and treating “failure” as a positive outcome—a learning opportunity rather than a personal defeat.

Shifting to a data-aware framework requires examining how product and design decisions have been made. If decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, those people must understand and recognize the value of bringing user data into the process, because their individual weight will diminish—as will the weight of any single opinion. This transition demands that individuals separate their ego from their ideas and prioritize customer outcomes over personal credit. It also prompts self-reflection: are you comfortable seeing how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process? Embracing data means accepting that your intuition, however experienced, may be wrong, and that the ultimate arbiter is the user’s behavior, not your conviction.
